# Automation & Workforce Transition Roadmap
### A five-site network conversion, staged for optionality rather than certainty

*A note on how this is written: I've built this as a sequence of decisions with explicit gates rather than a fixed plan. The numbers below are illustrative placeholders — swap in your actuals and most of the logic holds. Where I've left a question open, it's because the answer lives with the people running the docks, not with me.*

---

## 1. The framing question nobody has asked yet

The vendors are selling you a labor-substitution story. Your actual problem may be a *variance* story: 35% turnover means roughly a third of your pickers are always on the learning curve, which is almost certainly where the errors that are damaging key accounts are coming from. Automation that reduces headcount but keeps a churning workforce buys you a smaller version of the same problem.

Worth sitting with: if you could stabilize turnover at 15% and hold error rates at target, how much of the automation business case would still be compelling? My hunch is *most of it, but not all of it, and not everywhere.* That distinction is what makes this affordable.

And the competitor's failure is instructive precisely because it wasn't a technology failure. Big-bang cutovers fail when the experienced people who could have improvised through the chaos have already been told they're redundant. **Sequence the people commitments ahead of the steel.**

---

## 2. Site segmentation: automate to fit, not to a standard

Before committing capital, score each site on seven axes. This takes about six weeks with a small team and a decent WMS extract.

| Axis | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Order profile (eaches vs. cases vs. pallets; lines/order) | Determines whether goods-to-person even pays |
| SKU velocity curve | A steep curve favors modular AMR + pick-to-light; a flat long tail favors dense storage automation |
| Building physics (clear height, columns, floor flatness, dock count) | Kills more automation business cases than economics does |
| Real estate horizon (owned vs. lease expiry) | Never sink 8-figure fixed automation into a lease with <10 years left |
| Local labor market tightness & wage trajectory | The real driver of payback |
| Customer concentration & service sensitivity | Determines conversion risk tolerance |
| Community/employment concentration | Determines the *pace* you're allowed to move |

### Illustrative segmentation

| Site | Profile | Automation degree | Wave |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DC-2** (mid-size, ~220 staff, tight urban labor market, worst error rate, high turnover) | High-velocity eaches | **Level 2** — AMR-assisted picking, subscription model + process foundation | Wave 1 (pilot) |
| **DC-4** (large, ~380 staff, mixed profile, owned, good building) | Broad, long tail | **Level 3** — AMR + goods-to-person for the C-movers, automated print-and-apply, sortation refresh | Wave 2 |
| **DC-1** (anchor site, ~500 staff, main employer in town, owned, tall clear height) | Highest volume, key accounts | **Level 3–4**, but framed as *capacity expansion*, not displacement | Wave 3 |
| **DC-3** (~250 staff, aging building, lease expiry in 6 yrs, low density) | Case/pallet-heavy | **Level 0–1 only** — engineering, slotting, voice picking, powered equipment. No fixed automation. | Wave 1 (parallel, cheap) |
| **DC-5** (smallest, ~150 staff, overlapping catchment with DC-4) | Regional overflow | **Strategic question, not an automation question** — candidate to convert to a cross-dock / returns & value-added-services node | Wave 4 decision |

The temptation will be to start with DC-1 because that's where the biggest absolute savings sit. I'd resist it firmly. Starting where the stakes are highest is how you end up on the national news.

---

## 3. The automation ladder — buy the smallest rung that clears the bar

**Level 0 — Engineering & process (Months 0–9, all sites).** Re-slotting to velocity, batch/cluster picking, pick-path optimization, voice or vision picking, labor standards with a real LMS, error root-cause analysis, ergonomic fixes. Typical result: 12–20% productivity, 30–50% error reduction, capital in the low hundreds of thousands per site. This is the highest-ROI work in the entire program and it happens to also be the work that makes any subsequent automation actually perform. Skipping it is how vendors end up automating your bad process at high speed.

**Level 1 — Light mechanization.** Conveyor/sortation refresh, print-and-apply, autonomous tuggers, powered carts. Modest capital, easily relocated.

**Level 2 — Collaborative AMRs.** Robot-assisted picking, ideally on a robots-as-a-service or lease structure. This is the key strategic choice: it converts capital risk into operating cost, scales in units of one, redeploys across sites, and requires almost nothing of the building. Expect 1.6–2.3x pick rate and a large drop in walking-driven fatigue and error. It is also *reversible*, which is worth more than the vendors will price it at.

**Level 3 — Goods-to-person.** Cube/shuttle storage for the slow-moving tail, decant and induction. Heavy capital, real payback, real lock-in. Only at owned sites with the right cube profile and a decade-plus horizon.

**Level 4 — Deep integration.** Robotic each-picking, automated packing, palletizing. Adopt selectively and late; the technology is improving faster than your payback period.

---

## 4. Sequencing: four waves, five gates

**Wave 0 — Foundation (Months 0–6).**
Data integrity, baseline lock (see §7), Level 0 engineering at all five sites, WMS/WES readiness assessment, and — critically — the public workforce compact (§5) *before* any vendor contract is announced. Also: a network-wide hiring policy change, described below.

**Wave 1 — Prove it where it's cheap to be wrong (Months 4–16).**
DC-2 goes Level 2 on a subscription. DC-3 gets Level 0–1 in parallel as a control group. Convert 15% of volume first — one velocity band or one non-critical customer segment — run dual-path for six weeks, then step up. Gate review at Month 14.

**Wave 2 — Scale the pattern (Months 12–30).**
DC-4 replicates DC-2's AMR deployment (now with your own trained people leading it, not the vendor's) and adds a GTP module for the long tail. Second gate at Month 28.

**Wave 3 — The anchor site, framed as growth (Months 26–46).**
DC-1 gets the deepest automation — but the design brief is *absorb network volume and grow throughput per square foot*, not *remove people*. If DC-5 is consolidated or repurposed in the same window, its volume lands at DC-1, and DC-1's automation covers work that was previously done elsewhere. Headcount at DC-1 can then stay roughly flat, or decline only at the pace of natural attrition, while the network's total cost per unit drops. That's the sequence that keeps the town whole and keeps you out of the news.

**Wave 4 — Network reshape (Months 40–60).**
DC-5 decision executes. DC-3 lease decision executes. Residual automation top-ups where the data has earned them.

**The gates.** No capital releases for wave N+1 until wave N has held, for two consecutive months: ≥85% of modeled throughput at design conditions, error rate at or below target, and service level at or above pre-conversion baseline. Pre-agree the kill criteria in writing, before the first purchase order. A program that cannot be stopped is not a program, it's a commitment.

---

## 5. The workforce architecture — where your 35% turnover becomes an asset

The uncomfortable arithmetic, said plainly: at 35% annual turnover, a 220-person site loses ~77 people a year. If automation removes 30% of labor hours (~66 roles), **attrition alone covers the reduction inside twelve months** — provided you stop backfilling *before* go-live, not after.

So the single most important workforce lever is a scheduling decision: **freeze external hiring at each site 6–9 months ahead of its conversion, and bridge the gap with temporary/flex labor that you can release without harm.** Temps become the shock absorber; permanent employees become the protected class. This is the mechanism that lets you make a genuine no-layoff commitment and mean it.

### The compact (announce it first, in writing)

1. **No involuntary separation of a permanent employee as a direct result of automation** at any converted site, for 24 months post-go-live.
2. **First right of refusal** on every new role created, with paid training on the clock.
3. **Published pay ladder** for the new roles, with the increases visible up front.
4. Employees participate in vendor selection and pilot design. Not as a courtesy — as a design input, because they know where the process actually breaks.
5. If a site is ever consolidated, **notice far beyond WARN minimums** (I'd target 9–12 months), plus the package in §5.3.

### 5.2 The role ladder

| From | To | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Picker | Robotics operator / flow ambassador | Tier 1, +8–12% |
| Picker | Exception & problem-solve handler | The highest-judgment floor role; recruit your best troubleshooters |
| Picker / QA | Inventory integrity & quality auditor | Directly attacks the key-account error problem |
| Any | Maintenance Tech I → II → Controls Tech | +30–70%; use a registered apprenticeship — often partly subsidized, and it's a credential the person keeps |
| Lead | WES/systems analyst, trainer, CI specialist | Build a train-the-trainer core so you're not renting vendor expertise forever |

Selection on demonstrated aptitude, with tenure as tie-breaker. Publish the criteria. Long-tenured employees are frequently the strongest candidates for exception handling and quality work — the roles that require knowing why things go wrong — so this isn't charity, it's talent allocation.

### 5.3 Where reduction is genuinely unavoidable

Voluntary separation packages offered *first* and generously (you'll often over-subscribe); early-retirement bridges for tenured staff near eligibility; transfer with relocation support; extended healthcare; severance scaled to tenure; outplacement with regional employer partnerships lined up *before* announcement. For DC-1's town specifically: a community transition fund, advance engagement with the mayor and the local college, and a commitment that the site's total wage bill doesn't fall even if headcount eventually does.

Engage any union or works council before design freeze, not after. A joint technology committee with real information rights costs you very little and removes the adversarial framing that turned the competitor's rollout into a story.

---

## 6. Holding service while you convert

The rules I'd treat as non-negotiable:

- **No conversion inside peak.** Cutover windows in the trough only.
- **Slice, don't flip.** Migrate by velocity class or customer segment, 10–15% of volume at a time, with dual-path running until the new path outperforms the old on both rate *and* accuracy.
- **Ring-fence the key accounts.** Name them. They stay on the proven process until the new one has demonstrably beaten the baseline. Tell them what you're doing before they notice — a customer who was briefed is an ally; one who discovers it via a mispick is not.
- **Inventory accuracy gate.** No go-live below 99.5% location accuracy. Cycle-count blitz beforehand.
- **Relief valve.** Contracted 3PL overflow, mothballed space, or a sister-DC forward deployment held on standby for each conversion window. Budget it as insurance, not waste.
- **Graceful degradation by design.** Every automated zone must retain a manual fallback capable of running at ≥50% throughput. Write it into the vendor spec.
- **Hypercare.** Six to eight weeks, war room, daily standing review, pre-authorized service credits, and a written rollback plan with a named decision-maker and a time limit.

---

## 7. Measuring whether this is actually working

**Lock a 12-month baseline before Wave 0 touches anything.** Without it, every subsequent argument becomes unresolvable.

| Domain | Metric | Cadence |
|---|---|---|
| **Financial** | Fully loaded cost per unit / per line shipped | Monthly |
| | Labor hours per line, by zone | Weekly |
| | Actual vs. modeled payback, by wave | Quarterly gate |
| | True TCO: maintenance, spares, software, energy, downtime, vendor support | Quarterly |
| **Operational** | UPH by zone; throughput at peak vs. design capacity | Weekly |
| | Mispicks per million; order accuracy by key account | Weekly |
| | On-time ship %, dock-to-stock, order cycle time | Daily/weekly |
| | System uptime, MTBF, MTTR | Weekly |
| | Inventory location accuracy | Monthly |
| **Workforce** | Voluntary turnover (the headline number — target sub-18% at converted sites) | Monthly |
| | Involuntary separations attributable to automation (**target: zero**) | Monthly |
| | Time-to-proficiency for new hires | Monthly |
| | % workforce certified Tier 2+; internal fill rate | Quarterly |
| | TRIR / recordable injuries | Monthly |
| | Engagement pulse — short, frequent, and actually read | Quarterly |
| **Customer** | Chargebacks/deductions by account; scorecard performance; retention | Monthly |
| **Community** | Local headcount and wage bill at DC-1 | Quarterly |

Two disciplines that separate real programs from theatrical ones:

**Bank the savings.** Re-baseline site budgets the quarter after each go-live, so the benefit shows up in the P&L instead of quietly dissolving into overtime and temp spend.
